html:
Company: E-bikes producer · Home country: Italy · Size: Small (<50 staff) · HS 871160 (Vehicles & transport equipment) · Trade data 2019-2024

1. Executive Summary

Verdict: DO NOT ENTER NOW. Limited attractiveness at present; monitor and revisit.

Market attractiveness: 4.1/10
Recommended entry mode: Indirect / direct exporting via importers and distributors

  • Import market of $3.31 m in 2024, trend growth -26.1% a year (data confidence: low).
  • Supply is highly concentrated (HHI 2,568); top supplier India holds 34.04%.
  • CAGE distance from Italy: high.
  • Applicable import duty: 45% (MFN rate (no free-trade agreement)); landed cost ≈ +61% over ex-works price before VAT.
  • Italy is supplier #15 with 0.17% of imports.
  • EU-27 suppliers hold 4.59% of China's imports.

2. Market Size & Growth

Market size is measured as imports into China (UN Comtrade (China-reported imports, excluding re-imports of Chinese goods)). Imports show demand served from abroad, not total consumption.

Year Imports (USD)
2019 $355.32 k
2020 $7.83 m
2021 $10.34 m
2022 $3.86 m
2023 $2.79 m
2024 $3.31 m

Growth 2020-2024: trend -26.15% a year (log-linear fit over all years); end-point CAGR -19.35%.

Data confidence: Low. The growth signal in the score is shrunk towards neutral because:

  • Series break: values before 2020 are near zero, likely a classification change or reporting gap, so growth is measured from 2020.
  • Small market (below 50 million): a few shipments can swing growth rates strongly.

Market average unit value: $44.63/kg. Unit values show each supplier's price level (product mix also matters).

HHI 2,568: Highly concentrated. A few suppliers dominate, so a newcomer must win share from incumbents or exploit buyers' wish to diversify supply (EU 'de-risking').

The EU-27's share of China's imports moved from 27.66% (2019) to 4.59% (2024).

Your starting position: Italy

  • Supplier #15 of 20 with 0.17% of imports in 2024 (-3.37 pp since 2019).

4. PESTEL Analysis

  • Political: One-party state with active industrial policy (Made in China 2025, dual circulation). Geopolitical tension with the EU and US; retaliation risk in trade disputes (e.g. EU brandy, pork, dairy probes). Vehicles are a flashpoint in EU-China trade policy.
  • Economic: World's second-largest economy and a huge consumer market, but slower growth, weak consumer confidence and strong price competition from domestic champions. Latest: GDP growth 5.0% (2025), inflation 0.1% (World Bank).
  • Social: Digitally native consumers; 'guochao' preference for domestic brands among younger buyers; foreign brands win on safety, heritage and premium positioning.
  • Technological: World-leading e-commerce and super-apps (Tmall, JD, Douyin, WeChat); fast product cycles; strong domestic manufacturing capability.
  • Environmental: Dual-carbon goals (peak 2030, neutrality 2060) drive demand for clean-tech; growing ESG disclosure requirements. Electrification targets support EV and e-mobility demand.
  • Legal: Foreign Investment Law (2020) improved access; still complex licensing, local standards (GB/CCC), data-localisation rules and uneven IP enforcement.

5. CAGE Distance

Dimension Distance Evidence
Cultural High Different language families (Romance vs Sinitic); localisation needed.
Administrative High No EU-China FTA: MFN tariffs, CCC/GB standards, distinct legal system and growing trade tension.
Geographic High ~8,125 km between capitals. Long lead times (Asia-Europe sea freight ~30-45 days; China-Europe rail ~15-20 days).
Economic High GDP per capita $43,309 (home) vs $13,862 (target), ratio 3.1x.

Overall distance: High.

6. Tariffs, Trade Defence & Regulation

Import duty

  • MFN applied tariff of China: 45%, 2023 (World Bank WITS / UNCTAD TRAINS (MFN applied, simple average)).
  • Likely rate for a company from Italy: 45% (MFN rate (no free-trade agreement)).

⚠️ Trade policy note (checked 2026-11-21): EU anti-dumping and anti-subsidy duties on e-bikes from China have applied since 2019 (check the current rate and any expiry review). Official source.

Indicative landed cost (per 100 of ex-works value)

Item Amount Assumption
Goods (ex-works) 100.00
Freight & insurance 10.00 10% for high distance
Import duty 49.50 45% on CIF value
Clearance, broker, port 1.50 1.5%
Import VAT 20.73 13% (China), usually recoverable for VAT-registered importers
Landed cost 181.74 161.00 before VAT (+61.0%)

China also levies consumption tax on cars and some cosmetics; add it to the model where relevant.

Regulatory checklist

  • CCC certification and MIIT product catalogue listing for vehicles; CCC for electric bicycles (GB 17761 standard)
  • Domestic producers dominate EVs and e-bikes; intense price competition
  • Customs registration of the consignee; Chinese-language labelling for retail goods
  • Foreign Investment Law (2020) and the Negative List: most sectors open to wholly foreign-owned enterprises (WFOE)
  • Data Security Law and Personal Information Protection Law (PIPL) for any customer data collected
  • Cross-border e-commerce (e.g. Tmall Global, JD Worldwide) allows testing demand under a lighter regime for many consumer goods

Official texts: CNCA: China Compulsory Certification (CCC) · General Administration of Customs (GACC) · MOFCOM: foreign investment and the Negative List

Regulatory notes compiled 2026-11-21 from official sources; not legal advice.

Verify current duties and requirements: - China Customs tariff and regulations (GACC) - MOFCOM trade remedy notices - EU Access2Markets: China export requirements - EU SME Centre (China market guides)

7. Risk Matrix

Risk Likelihood Impact Mitigation
High import tariff (45% applicable) High Medium Price the duty into the landed cost; consider local assembly, a bonded warehouse or sourcing from an FTA partner.
Dominant incumbent supplier (India, 34.04% share) High High Differentiate on quality, service, sustainability and EU/China-specific certification rather than price.
Shrinking import demand High Medium Target growing niches or member states; validate demand before fixed investment.
Trade-defence or retaliation measures in the EU-China corridor High High Monitor trade-defence notices; diversify sourcing and production locations; build tariff scenarios into pricing.
Institutional and IP-protection risk Medium High Register trademarks and patents locally before entry; use contracts with local arbitration (e.g. CIETAC/HKIAC).
Logistics disruption (Red Sea, port congestion, freight-rate swings) Medium Medium Use mixed sea/rail routing, safety stock in a regional hub, Incoterms that share freight risk.
Brand and message mis-fit with local consumers Medium Medium Local consumer testing, native-language content, local marketplace and social channels.
Thin or volatile trade data: market size and growth are uncertain Medium Medium Validate demand with distributor interviews and a small pilot before committing budget.
Currency volatility (EUR/CNY/USD) Medium Medium Price in home currency where possible; hedge large contracts with forwards.

8. Recommended Entry Mode

Indirect / direct exporting via importers and distributors

  • Moderate attractiveness or high distance favour a low-commitment, reversible entry.
  • Keeps capital at risk low while you learn the market.
  • Your home country is not yet an established supplier here: buyers will need proof of quality, so plan for samples, certification and references.
  • Inputs: attractiveness 4.1/10, CAGE distance high, institutional quality 4.8/10, company size small (<50 staff).

9. Attractiveness Score Breakdown

Component Weight Score
Market size 25% 1.0/10
Growth 25% 2.5/10
Competitive openness 20% 7.4/10
Institutional quality 15% 4.8/10
Logistics 15% 6.8/10
Total 4.1/10

Sensitivity to the weights

The weights are a judgement call, so the same sub-scores are re-weighted under alternative schemes:

Weighting scheme Score
Base case 4.1
Equal weights 4.5
Size-led (large incumbents) 3.4
Growth-led (start-ups) 4.0
Risk-averse (institutions first) 4.5
Niche entrant (openness first) 5.0

Weight-sensitive: the score ranges from 3.4 to 5.0 and crosses a verdict threshold (do not enter now, enter with caution), so treat the verdict as borderline.

10. 90-Day Action Plan

  1. Days 1-30, validate: confirm the HS code and duty rate on official tariff tools, size the niche with customer interviews, shortlist 10 potential partners or channels in China.
  2. Days 1-30, compliance: map required certifications and labelling (see section 6), get quotes from a test lab or regulatory agent, register trademarks in the target market.
  3. Days 31-60, commercial model: build a landed-cost and pricing model (duties, freight, VAT, channel margins, FX), and draft the partner or channel agreement.
  4. Days 31-60, go-to-market: localise product pages, packaging and sales material; pick 1-2 launch channels consistent with the entry mode: indirect / direct exporting via importers and distributors.
  5. Days 61-90, pilot: ship a pilot order or open the online store, track sell-through, margin and customer feedback against go/no-go KPIs.

Sources

  • UN Comtrade (China-reported imports, excluding re-imports of Chinese goods), trade data 2019-2024
  • World Bank WITS / UNCTAD TRAINS (MFN tariffs)
  • World Bank World Development Indicators, Logistics Performance Index, Worldwide Governance Indicators
  • Regulatory notes: curated from official EU and Chinese sources; verify with the links in section 6
  • Frameworks: PESTEL; CAGE distance (Ghemawat, 2001); HHI bands (US DOJ/FTC 2023); entry-mode logic (Dunning's OLI, transaction-cost theory)
